I am a 50-year-old farmer in Quzhou County, and I have been working this land since I was a teenager. I only finished primary school, but I know what works here. Every year, I grow winter wheat followed by summer maize — that is the double-cropping system everyone in our village uses. The climate and soil on the North China Plain are suited to it, and it gives me both grain for my family and cash income from selling the surplus.

This year, I will plant wheat on my entire 8 mu plot in early October, right after the National Day holiday. I will use an improved wheat variety — the same kind my neighbors buy from the seed store in town. Before sowing, I will run the rotary tiller through the field to break up the maize stubble and prepare a good seedbed. For fertilizer, I will spread one bag of compound fertilizer per mu as basal dressing, and then topdress with urea at the wheat jointing stage in spring. I have learned that wheat needs water at critical times, so I will irrigate three times: once before winter to help the seedlings survive the cold, once at jointing, and once at heading. I will spray pesticides about four times in total — mainly for weeds, aphids, and the fungal diseases that show up when the weather turns humid.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, I will immediately plant summer maize. There is no time to waste because the frost comes early, so I will use no-tillage planting — I just drill the hybrid maize seeds directly into the wheat stubble. The seed dealer always recommends hybrid varieties like Nongda or Denghai, and they yield well. I will put down compound fertilizer at planting, and then irrigate twice: once when the maize is silking and once during grain filling. Maize pests are fewer than wheat, but I will still spray three times for insects and weeds.

I expect about 500 kg of wheat per mu and about 550 kg of maize per mu. That is a normal year for me. I do not grow cotton or vegetables — they need too much labor and too many chemicals, and the prices are unpredictable. Wheat and maize are stable. This is what I have always done, and this is what I will do again.
